interactions.label: Cancer stem cells hiding in the G0 phase are highly susceptible to most chemothe

params.question: Cancer stem cells hiding in the G0 phase are highly susceptible to most chemotherapy agents.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: G0 is actually a protected resting phase. Cells here are not actively dividing, so most chemotherapy drugs cannot reach them. The narration specifically noted that cancer stem cells hide in G0 to escape treatment — this is one of the key reasons for tumour recurrence.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. G0 cells are not actively dividing, so chemotherapy drugs that target cell-cycle processes — DNA synthesis, mitosis — cannot kill them effectively. Cancer stem cells exploit this resting phase to escape treatment, which is a major reason tumours recur even after apparently successful chemotherapy.

interactions.label: A patient on mercaptopurine for maintenance chemotherapy develops hyperuricaemia

params.question: A patient on mercaptopurine for maintenance chemotherapy develops hyperuricaemia and allopurinol is considered. Why must the mercaptopurine dose be reduced before adding allopurinol?

answers.text: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which also metabolises mercaptopurine, risking severe myelosuppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme responsible for breaking down mercaptopurine. Allopurinol blocks this enzyme, causing mercaptopurine to accumulate to toxic levels. The dose must be reduced to approximately one-third to prevent dangerous bone marrow suppression.

answers.text: Allopurinol displaces mercaptopurine from plasma protein binding sites, increasing free drug levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Protein-binding displacement is not the mechanism here. Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase — the same enzyme that breaks down mercaptopurine — leading to drug accumulation and severe myelosuppression.

answers.text: Allopurinol enhances renal tubular reabsorption of mercaptopurine, reducing its clearance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allopurinol does not affect renal tubular handling of mercaptopurine. The interaction occurs because allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for mercaptopurine breakdown, causing toxic accumulation.

answers.text: Allopurinol converts mercaptopurine into a nephrotoxic metabolite that damages the kidneys

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mercaptopurine is not converted to a nephrotoxic metabolite. Rather, allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase — the enzyme that normally inactivates mercaptopurine — causing the drug to accumulate and suppress the bone marrow.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key fact is that allopurinol and mercaptopurine share the same metabolic enzyme, xanthine oxidase. Blocking this enzyme with allopurinol prevents mercaptopurine breakdown, leading to dangerous accumulation and bone marrow suppression.
Well done. This is one of the most clinically important drug interactions in oncology — always reduce the mercaptopurine dose when co-prescribing allopurinol.

interactions.label: A patient receiving high-dose cyclophosphamide is prescribed MESNA for uroprotec

params.question: A patient receiving high-dose cyclophosphamide is prescribed MESNA for uroprotection. Which pharmacological property of MESNA allows it to prevent haemorrhagic cystitis without reducing the anticancer effect?

answers.text: It blocks cyclophosphamide absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MESNA does not affect cyclophosphamide absorption. It works downstream in the urinary tract, where its sulfhydryl group binds acrolein — the toxic metabolite — after it has been filtered into the urine.

answers.text: It remains inactive in the bloodstream and is activated only in the urine, where its sulfhydryl group binds acrolein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. MESNA is inactive while circulating in the blood and becomes activated only in urine. There, its free sulfhydryl group binds acrolein — the bladder-toxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide — converting it to a harmless thioether. This selective activation is why it protects the bladder without blunting the drug's tumour-killing activity.

answers.text: It competitively inhibits cyclophosphamide uptake by tumour cells, redirecting it away from the bladder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MESNA does not interact with tumour-cell drug uptake. It acts exclusively in the urinary tract, neutralising acrolein after it has been produced by hepatic metabolism and excreted by the kidneys.

answers.text: It accelerates hepatic conversion of cyclophosphamide to a less toxic form before it reaches the kidneys

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MESNA does not alter hepatic metabolism of cyclophosphamide. It works downstream — in the urine — binding and neutralising acrolein after the toxic metabolite has already been produced and filtered by the kidneys.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: MESNA is inactive in the blood and switches on only in the urine. Its sulfhydryl group binds acrolein there, converting it to a harmless thioether. This selective activation is what makes it an ideal uroprotectant — it never interferes with the anticancer effect.

Excellent. MESNA's selective urothelial activation is a textbook example of organ-targeted toxicity prevention — it is given at 60% of the cyclophosphamide dose, in three divided doses over eight hours, alongside IV hydration.

interactions.label: In the FOLFOX regimen for metastatic colon cancer, leucovorin is combined with 5

params.question: In the FOLFOX regimen for metastatic colon cancer, leucovorin is combined with 5-fluorouracil. What is the pharmacological role of leucovorin in this specific combination?

answers.text: It rescues normal cells from 5-fluorouracil toxicity, similar to its role with methotrexate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the most common misconception. With methotrexate, leucovorin does rescue normal cells by bypassing the blocked enzyme. But with 5-fluorouracil it plays the opposite role — it enhances the anticancer effect by stabilising the inhibitory complex on thymidylate synthase.

answers.text: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase to potentiate 5-fluorouracil's cytotoxicity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition is methotrexate's mechanism, not leucovorin's. With 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin acts as a cofactor that stabilises the ternary complex of 5-FU with thymidylate synthase, prolonging enzyme inhibition.

answers.text: It stabilises the ternary complex with thymidylate synthase, enhancing 5-fluorouracil's anticancer action

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Leucovorin provides the folate cofactor that locks 5-fluorouracil onto thymidylate synthase in a stable ternary complex, prolonging enzyme inhibition. This is the opposite of its rescue role with methotrexate — a distinction the video specifically flagged as commonly confused.

answers.text: It prevents oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy in the FOLFOX regimen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Leucovorin has no protective effect against oxaliplatin neuropathy. There is no established neuroprotective drug for oxaliplatin; management relies on avoiding cold exposure acutely, and dose reduction or discontinuation when cumulative sensory neuropathy becomes severe.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction: with methotrexate, leucovorin rescues normal cells by bypassing the blocked enzyme. With 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin enhances the anticancer effect by stabilising the ternary complex with thymidylate synthase. Same drug, opposite roles depending on the combination.

Well done. Leucovorin plays two completely different roles depending on context: rescue with methotrexate, but enhancement with 5-fluorouracil. This is a high-yield distinction for both exams and clinical practice.
